title: Signature Neighbourhood Net Charter
body:
The Signature Neighbourhood Net Charter is an original Signature design for a one-page founding agreement: the network belongs to its members, any member may inspect the accounts and the map, no funder buys control, and any member may leave with their data and without penalty. The Charter is read aloud at the founding meeting, signed by the first stewards, and displayed in the hall, so that later arguments can be settled by pointing at the wall rather than by remembering who promised what. The design is labeled Signature throughout.

How to do it: State member ownership in one page; Guarantee inspection of accounts and map; Bar funders from buying control; Guarantee exit with data and without penalty; Read aloud at founding and display in the hall.

What to check: Test the Charter by asking a new member to find the exit clause and the inspection right without help, and confirm both are found in a minute.

When to stop or get help: Do not adopt a charter that any founding member cannot explain. A charter that needs a lawyer to read is not a neighbourhood agreement.

Put it into practice on a small, low-stakes example first, so the routine is familiar before you need it under pressure. For this record, that means trying the steps once in a calm moment, with no deadline and no audience, and noticing which step feels hardest. The hardest step is usually the one worth practising twice, because pressure does not create new skills, it reveals the ones you have already rehearsed. Write down what you checked and what you found, because a check that leaves no note is hard to repeat and harder to trust later, and because a short note lets someone else pick up where you left off.

Share the routine with the people who will use it with you, so that stopping, checking, and asking for help are normal steps, not signs of failure. Agree in advance what you will do when a check fails, so that a failed check leads to a pause and a fix rather than an argument or a quiet decision to carry on anyway. Review the routine after a month of use and change the parts that did not work in practice, keeping the parts that did. A routine that is reviewed stays alive; a routine that is never reviewed slowly becomes a poster on a wall.

print('charter adopted:', signed == clauses)

title: Signature Volunteer Circle
body:
The Signature Volunteer Circle is an original Signature design for roles as a circle, not a hierarchy: organiser, installer, treasurer, and supporter sit as equals, each paired with a partner, and each role carries a written one-paragraph description that any member can read. The Circle meets monthly, rotates the chair, and recruits deliberately for non-technical members, because a circle of technicians is a club, not a community. The design is labeled Signature throughout.

How to do it: Four equal roles with one-paragraph descriptions; Every role paired with a partner; Monthly circle meetings with rotating chair; Deliberate recruitment of non-technical members; Roles published to all members.

What to check: Test the Circle by asking any member to name all four roles and their holders, and confirm the answer comes without checking a private chat.

When to stop or get help: Do not let any role sit with one unpaired person for more than a season. Unpaired roles are single points of failure wearing a title.

title: Signature Host Handshake

title: Signature Council of Stewards

When to stop or get help: Do not let the Council change the Charter alone. A council that can rewrite its own limits is no longer a council.

title: Signature Repair Rota Board
body:

When to stop or get help: Do not add a node to the Board without naming its checker. An unnamed node is an unmaintained node with a label.

title: Signature Growth Ladder
body:
The Signature Growth Ladder is an original Signature design for expansion as rungs, not leaps: each new street is a rung that requires the previous rung to be maintained, supported, and governed, with volunteers, sites, permissions, spares, and funds checked before climbing. What to check: Test the Ladder by attempting a second street while the first has an unchecked node, and confirm the Ladder refuses the climb.

When to stop or get help: Do not climb while maintenance lags. A ladder climbed on a broken rung falls on the climber and the community below.
